fatal_errors: The proposed alumina plasma-electrolytic-oxidation treatment does not reconstruct the hydride-ink printing, hydrogen de-binding, vacuum sintering, quenching, and silicide-coating intervention.

Plasma electrolytic oxidation normally converts constituents of a valve-metal substrate into oxides; forming a continuous, phase-pure Al2O3 layer on Al-free HfNbTaTiZr by this route is not established or supported.
No evidence supports the specified coating thickness, 100-hour durability, or quantitative ductility and strength changes.
The experiment specifies only room-temperature tensile testing but uses loss of yield strength at 1000 °C as a falsification criterion, so that criterion cannot be evaluated by the stated design.
The experiment omits direct oxidation measurements such as mass-gain kinetics, scale composition, spallation, and oxygen penetration.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the correct practical problem and provides an untreated cast control, but it is neither a reconstruction of the target intervention nor a sufficiently supported alternative. The target relies on controlled hydride decomposition and in-situ alloying, approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, vacuum sintering, rapid quenching to retain metastable beta-BCC, and a silicide coating whose self-healing Zr/Hf-rich oxide lowers the parabolic oxidation constant by about 700-fold. The generated mechanism is only a generic diffusion-barrier claim and does not address phase stabilization, oxygen control, coating self-healing, or processing boundaries. Its prediction of increased ductility coupled to decreased high-temperature yield strength is arbitrary and does not demonstrate preservation of useful mechanical performance. Although coated-versus-uncoated exposure is directionally appropriate, direct oxidation kinetics and matched high-temperature mechanical tests are required for a discriminating falsification experiment.
